Neonates of the bigeye thresher emerge at a precaudal length of approximately 69.6 cm [Lb = approximately 69.6 cm], a measurement derived from near-term embryos and freshly born free-swimming pups encountered in gillnet surveys throughout the tropical Atlantic. This relatively large birth size, typical of alopiid sharks, reflects an extended period of yolk-dependent embryonic development within the gravid female and confers an immediate advantage in evading the gape-limited predators that threaten smaller elasmobranchs upon parturition. Adult females ultimately attain a much greater ultimate precaudal length, reaching 224.6 cm [Li = 224.6 cm], while their male counterparts exhibit a slightly smaller maximum size, with the ultimate precaudal length recorded at 218.8 cm [Li = 218.8 cm] for males. This moderate sexual dimorphism in maximum body length is consistent with what has been documented in congeneric species such as Alopias vulpinus, and it likely arises from sex-specific energetic allocation strategies after the onset of gonadal maturation.

Sexual maturation in females of this species occurs when they reach a precaudal length at puberty of 177.7 cm [Lp = 177.7 cm], a value corroborated by total length estimates ranging between 332 and 341 cm from fisheries-dependent sampling across the western Indian Ocean. In contrast, males become reproductively mature at a substantially smaller body size, achieving puberty at a precaudal length of 150 cm [Lp = 150 cm] for males. This disparity in size at maturation between the sexes is biologically meaningful: it indicates that male bigeye threshers are capable of successfully copulating and fertilising ova at a significantly younger age and smaller body dimension than females, which must invest additional somatic growth before initiating the energetic demands of gestation. The corresponding body masses at these developmental landmarks reflect the different growth trajectories, with females weighing approximately 116.5 kg [Wwp = approximately 116.5 kg] at the onset of puberty at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] and males weighing a considerably more modest 69.1 kg [Wwp = 69.1 kg] at puberty for males at 17 °C [T = 17 °C].

Fully grown adult females attain an ultimate wet weight of 222.8 kg [Wwi = 222.8 kg] at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a calculation derived from length-weight regressions fitted to specimens landed by longline fisheries operating in subtropical waters. Adult males, by contrast, reach a smaller terminal size, with their ultimate wet weight recorded at 190.5 kg [Wwi = 190.5 kg] at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This divergence in maximum body mass underscores the reproductive strategy typical of many lamniform sharks: larger females can accommodate more developing embryos and produce larger pups, thereby enhancing per-offspring survival. At the population level, these mass-at-length relationships also provide crucial input for estimating biomass removal by fisheries and for evaluating the species' vulnerability to overexploitation given its relatively slow growth rate and late maturation. The allometric equations underlying these estimates are well-supported by the extensive morphometric data collected during dedicated research cruises.

Reproduction in the bigeye thresher proceeds at a modest pace, with females producing between 2 and 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = between 2 and 4 pups per litter] following an inferred gestation period of approximately 12 months, resulting in a single litter produced each year [F_R_i = single litter produced each year]. These life-history parameters are characteristic of a K-selected strategy and are typical of the family Alopiidae, which generally exhibit low fecundity coupled with large offspring size. This entire reproductive schedule unfolds at a mean environmental temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the thermal regime that dominates the deep scattering layer where adults primarily forage. The low annual reproductive output renders the species particularly sensitive to elevated fishing mortality, as the population's intrinsic capacity to compensate for removals through increased fecundity is severely constrained by these fixed biological limits.

Under these same thermal conditions of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the species exhibits a maximum lifespan of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years], based on vertebral band-pair counts from archived specimens collected in the North Atlantic. Females reach sexual maturity at an average of about 12.8 years after birth [tp = about 12.8 years after birth] at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a protracted developmental period that reflects the considerable time required to attain the necessary body size for supporting pregnancy. Males mature more quickly, requiring an estimated 9.5 years after birth [tp = estimated 9.5 years after birth] for males at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] to reach puberty, a difference that suggests divergent growth rates and metabolic priorities between the sexes during the sub-adult phase. These delayed maturation schedules, which are among the most protracted recorded for any pelagic elasmobranch, position Alopias superciliosus alongside the Greenland shark and the basking shark in the slowest extreme of the continuum of life-history strategies observed in the class Chondrichthyes.
